query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Intermediate‐temperature thermal aging of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy induces nanoscale segregation of specific constituent elements at grain boundaries, which creates thin, brittle interfacial films that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote embrittlement. In contrast, a subsequent recovery (higher temperature) treatment can partly re-homogenize these segregated phases, restoring toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase, compositionally complex AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy with uniformly distributed elements.
generation.intervention: Apply intermediate-temperature thermal aging designed to promote grain boundary segregation and compare with a recovery treatment following aging.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at ambient and elevated service temperatures under controlled loading conditions (e.g., tensile and fracture toughness tests). The treatments (aging and recovery) should be performed under identical time–temperature profiles for reproducibility.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries resulting in thin brittle intergranular films.
generation.mechanism: During intermediate-temperature aging, diffusion processes cause one or more alloying elements to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, producing localized compositional deviations. These deviations form brittle films that compromise grain boundary cohesion, thus reducing toughness. A subsequent recovery treatment may allow for re-homogenization or coarsening of these segregates, mitigating embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the alloy after intermediate-temperature aging will exhibit significantly reduced toughness (lower ductility and fracture toughness) and microstructural evidence of grain-boundary segregation. The recovery-treated samples should show partial or complete restoration of toughness and a more homogeneous grain boundary composition.
generation.baseline: As-cast alloy with its initial, uniformly distributed microstructure and associated toughness values.
generation.boundary: Findings are expected within intermediate thermal aging conditions relevant to service temperatures and loadings typical for demanding engineering applications. If treatments occur outside these temperature/time regimes, effects might not be observable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent of segregation, the identity of the segregating elements critical to embrittlement, and the recovery treatment parameters required for re-homogenization are not yet quantified. Additionally, interplay with other microstructural features (e.g., residual stresses or subgrain formation) might modify the net effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: (1) as-cast baseline, (2) samples subjected to controlled intermediate-temperature thermal aging, and (3) samples receiving the same aging treatment followed by a recovery treatment. Conduct microstructural characterization (using transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography) to assess grain-boundary segregation and perform mechanical tests (tensile testing and fracture toughness evaluation) under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of grain-boundary composition and presence/thickness of any intergranular films
Fracture toughness and crack propagation behavior
Comparative analysis of the microstructure before and after recovery treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to intermediate-temperature aging do not show any statistically significant reduction in toughness (ductility and fracture toughness) compared to the as-cast baseline, and if no measurable grain-boundary segregation is detected, then the hypothesis—that such segregation induces brittleness in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys—is falsified.
